subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Nudging Medication Adherence
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Nudging Medication Adherence.

hook.text: Half of patients with chronic conditions don't take their meds as prescribed. The pills are there. The habit isn't.

buildup.text: Daily reminder texts, pill organizers, and simplified dosing schedules are nudges that boost adherence by up to 30%.

discovery.text: Volpp used lotteries: patients eligible for daily prizes if they took their meds had 40% higher adherence.

twist.text: The lottery prize was small ($100/month), but the daily anticipation kept medication salient.

climax.text: Medication adherence nudges save lives and billions in hospital costs. Small design changes prevent big health failures.

punchline.text: A text reminder can save a life.

quiz.question: How did lottery incentives improve medication adherence?
options: Daily anticipation of winning kept medication top of mind
Patients were penalized for missing doses

details.summary: Nudging medication adherence uses reminders, simplified packaging, and default prescription refills to help patients take medication consistently. Non-adherence is a massive public health problem driven by forgetfulness, complexity, and friction rather than deliberate refusal.
details.whyItMatters: Medication non-adherence costs hundreds of billions in preventable hospitalizations and deaths annually. The problem is not that patients refuse treatment but that they forget, get confused by complex regimens, or face friction in refilling.
takeaways: Non-adherence is primarily driven by friction and forgetting, not intentional refusal
Text reminders improve adherence rates by 10 to 15 percent
Simplified pill packaging and auto-refill defaults reduce barriers significantly

faq.question: Why is medication non-adherence such a widespread problem?
faq.answer: Taking medication consistently requires daily effort against no visible immediate reward. The benefits of adherence are invisible, the costs of skipping one dose seem negligible, and the friction of refilling prescriptions accumulates. Each small barrier compounds into major non-adherence.

faq.question: What nudge interventions most effectively improve medication adherence?
faq.answer: Auto-refill prescription defaults, simplified once-daily dosing, blister packaging with dates, text message reminders, and linking medication to existing habits like morning coffee. Each reduces a specific friction point in the adherence chain.
